popular.q1_question: What is the biggest festival in Cusco?
popular.q1_answer: Inti Raymi, the Festival of the Sun, is the largest and most famous theatrical reenactment of an ancient Inca ceremony.
popular.q2_question: Which month has the most festivals?
popular.q2_answer: June is a particularly busy month for festivals in Cusco, including the famous Inti Raymi and Corpus Christi.

inti-raymi.location_detail: Main events at Qorikancha, Plaza de Armas and Sacsayhuamán.
inti-raymi.description: The ancient Inca festival of the sun, a spectacular theatrical reenactment.
inti-raymi.longDescription: Inti Raymi, the "Festival of the Sun," was the most important religious ceremony of the Inca Empire in honor of the god Inti. Today, it is a massive theatrical representation held every year on June 24 in Cusco. It involves hundreds of actors in vibrant costumes, with historical rituals, dances, and processions that take place at Qorikancha, the Plaza de Armas, and the fortress of Sacsayhuamán.
inti-raymi.history: Originally established by the Inca Pachacuti in the 15th century, the festival marked the winter solstice and the start of the new year. It was banned by the Spanish in the 16th century but was revived in the 20th century as a theatrical event to honor Cusco's heritage.

traditions.tradition_1: Processions with traditional music
traditions.tradition_2: Symbolic sacrifice of a llama
traditions.tradition_3: Ritual offerings of chicha (corn beer)
traditions.tradition_4: Folkloric dances from the four suyus (regions) of the Inca Empire

schedule.event_1_desc: Ceremony begins at Qorikancha (Temple of the Sun).
schedule.event_2_desc: Procession moves to the Plaza de Armas for the "Encounter of the Times".
schedule.event_3_desc: Main ceremony at the esplanade of Sacsayhuamán.

corpus-christi.description: A massive religious procession where 15 saints and virgins parade through Cusco.
corpus-christi.longDescription: Corpus Christi in Cusco is a vibrant and unique syncretic festival, blending Catholic faith with ancient Andean traditions. Fifteen statues of saints and virgins from different parishes are carried in a grand procession to the Cusco Cathedral, where they 'visit' the body of Christ for eight days. The festival is famous for its elaborate decorations, music, and the traditional dish called Chiriuchu.
corpus-christi.history: Introduced by the Spanish in the 16th century, the festival was used to replace the Inca practice of parading ancestral mummies. The Andean people adapted the Catholic tradition, assigning their own sacred meanings to the saints, thus creating a powerful symbol of cultural resistance and fusion.

traditions.tradition_1: The entry of the 15 saints into the Plaza de Armas.
traditions.tradition_2: The consumption of 'Chiriuchu', a cold dish with various meats and ingredients.
traditions.tradition_3: Musical bands accompanying each saint.
traditions.tradition_4: The 'Octave of Corpus', where the saints return to their parishes a week later.

schedule.event_1_desc: Main procession of all saints and virgins around the Plaza de Armas.
schedule.event_2_desc: Gastronomic fairs in Plaza San Francisco to try Chiriuchu.
schedule.event_1_desc: Second procession as the saints return to their home parishes.

qoyllur-riti.description: A spiritual pilgrimage to the Sinakara Valley, blending Catholic and Andean beliefs.
qoyllur-riti.longDescription: Qoyllur Rit'i, or the "Snow Star Festival," is a centuries-old religious pilgrimage that takes place in the remote Sinakara Valley at the foot of Mount Ausangate. Tens of thousands of pilgrims from surrounding villages travel for days, bringing large crosses to the sanctuary. The festival is a unique syncretism of Catholic and Andean beliefs, celebrating the stars, the mountain spirits (Apus), and the Lord of Qoyllur Rit'i.
qoyllur-riti.history: The festival's origins are a blend of an 18th-century Catholic miracle story and ancient Andean mountain worship. It centers on the appearance of the Christ child to a young shepherd boy. It has been recognized by UNESCO as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

traditions.tradition_1: Night-long vigils with music and dance
traditions.tradition_2: Processions of "Ukukus" (bear-men dancers) to the glacier
traditions.tradition_3: Elaborate dance performances by different "nations" representing their communities
traditions.tradition_4: A final 24-hour procession for the Corpus Christi festival in Cusco

schedule.event_1_desc: Pilgrims arrive at Mahuayani, beginning the 8km walk to the sanctuary.
Main day of celebration with continuous music, dancing, and religious services.
"Serenata" concert for the Christ of Qoyllur Rit'i.
schedule.event_2_desc: Processions and farewell dances as pilgrims begin their journey home.

paucartambo-virgen-del-carmen.description: A vibrant and chaotic festival in the colonial town of Paucartambo with masked dancers.
paucartambo-virgen-del-carmen.longDescription: The festival in honor of the Virgen del Carmen is one of Peru's most celebrated and wild parties. For several days, the quiet colonial town of Paucartambo erupts in a riot of color, music, and dance. Troupes of masked dancers in spectacular costumes take over the streets, each representing different characters and stories from Peruvian history and folklore. The festival culminates in a procession where the statue of the Virgin blesses the town and battles costumed demons on the rooftops.
paucartambo-virgen-del-carmen.history: The devotion to the Virgen del Carmen (also known as Mamacha Carmen) dates back to the colonial era. Legend says her face miraculously appeared on a rock, and the festival grew around this veneration. The dances themselves are a syncretic mix of Catholic, Andean, and even Amazonian influences.

traditions.tradition_1: Parades of costumed dance troupes like Saqra (devils), Qhapaq Negro, and Maqta
traditions.tradition_2: Musical battles between different groups
traditions.tradition_3: Acrobatic displays and mock battles
traditions.tradition_4: The "burning" of the demons on the final day

schedule.event_1_desc: Fireworks and music mark the beginning of the festival.
schedule.event_2_desc: First appearance of the dance troupes in the main square.
schedule.event_1_desc: Main mass in honor of the Virgen del Carmen.
schedule.event_2_desc: Grand procession through the town streets with the statue of the Virgin.
schedule.event_1_desc: The battle between the angels and demons takes place, with demons performing acrobatics on the rooftops.

qeswachaka-bridge-festival.description: The annual reconstruction of the last Inca rope bridge.
qeswachaka-bridge-festival.longDescription: The Q'eswachaka Bridge Festival is an extraordinary example of living Inca heritage. Every year, four communities come together to rebuild this rope bridge using traditional techniques passed down for centuries. The four-day process is a communal ritual that involves ceremonies, work, and celebration, culminating in the crossing of the new bridge.
qeswachaka-bridge-festival.history: This tradition has been maintained for over 500 years, being a vital link for communication between communities. In 2013, the knowledge, techniques, and rituals associated with the reconstruction of the Q'eswachaka bridge were recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

traditions.tradition_1: Offering ceremony to the Apus.
traditions.tradition_2: Collection and braiding of 'q'oya' (vegetable fiber).
traditions.tradition_3: Dismantling of the old bridge.
traditions.tradition_4: Weaving and assembly of the new bridge by specialists.
traditions.tradition_5: Inaugural crossing with music and dance.

schedule.event_1_desc: Dismantling of the old ropes and weaving of the new ones.
schedule.event_2_desc: Assembly and installation of the new bridge.

linderaje-chinchero.description: Ritual combat to define communal boundaries.
linderaje-chinchero.longDescription: Linderaje is a ritual combat practice that takes place in Chinchero to settle land disputes between communities. Far from being a violent brawl, it is a regulated and symbolic confrontation that strengthens social ties and reaffirms territorial identity. It is a display of strength and community organization that ends with celebration, regardless of the outcome.
linderaje-chinchero.history: Of pre-Hispanic origin, these ritual battles were a way for communities to manage conflicts and demonstrate their vitality. The Spanish colonists tried to suppress them, but the tradition has endured, adapting over time and becoming a fundamental part of the local cultural calendar.

traditions.tradition_1: Confrontations by community representatives.
traditions.tradition_2: Use of traditional clothing and whips (warakas).
traditions.tradition_3: Presence of music and dance to encourage the fighters.
traditions.tradition_4: The fight ends with a communal agreement and celebration.

schedule.event_1_desc: The communities gather at the boundary lines to begin the ritual.

corpus-chinchero.description: Syncretic version of Corpus Christi with unique dances.
corpus-chinchero.longDescription: While Cusco city has its grand Corpus Christi, the version in Chinchero is more intimate and has its own personality. The saints are also paraded, but with a strong presence of local dances and music that give it a unique Andean character. It is a perfect example of how large religious festivals are adapted and reinterpreted in rural communities.
corpus-chinchero.history: Like the Corpus Christi of Cusco, it was established in colonial times, but in Chinchero it merged even more deeply with local agricultural and social celebrations. It became a space to reaffirm the identity of the Chinchero ayllus (kin groups).

traditions.tradition_1: Procession of the saints accompanied by traditional dances.
traditions.tradition_2: Gastronomic fair with typical dishes of the area.
traditions.tradition_3: Strong community participation.

schedule.event_1_desc: Main procession and dance presentation in the main square of Chinchero.

carnaval-de-tinta.description: A traditional and colorful carnival with competitive dances.
carnaval-de-tinta.longDescription: The Carnival of Tinta is one of the most recognized in the Cusco region for its competitive spirit. Different communities present their best dancers and musicians in a 'qhaswa' (celebratory competition) that fills the main square with energy and color. It's a celebration of abundance and fertility, with deep roots in Andean culture.
carnaval-de-tinta.history: Carnivals in the Andes are a syncretism of European pre-Lenten celebrations and Andean rituals of harvest and praise to the Pachamama (Mother Earth). Tinta has preserved a very traditional version of this festival.

traditions.tradition_1: Dance competitions between communities.
traditions.tradition_2: The 'Yunza' or 'Cortamonte,' where a tree laden with gifts is cut down.
traditions.tradition_3: Traditional food and drink.
traditions.tradition_4: Playful games with water and foam.

schedule.event_1_desc: Main competition of dance troupes in the Plaza de Armas of Tinta.

ollantaytambo-reyes.description: A procession of the Christ Child, 'Niño Jesús', through the ancient Inca town.
ollantaytambo-reyes.longDescription: The Adoration of the Magi in Ollantaytambo is a charming and solemn festival. It celebrates the journey of the Christ Child from the church of San Blas in Cusco to his temple in Marcacocha, near Ollantaytambo. The procession is accompanied by traditional dances and music, winding through the impressive Inca streets of the town.
ollantaytambo-reyes.history: This festival blends the Catholic celebration of the Epiphany with local Andean traditions. The devotion to the 'Niño de Marcacocha' is central to the identity of Ollantaytambo and its surrounding communities.

traditions.tradition_1: The main procession with the statue of the Christ Child.
traditions.tradition_2: Dances such as 'Huiloconas' and 'Mollos'.
traditions.tradition_3: Masses and religious services.

schedule.event_1_desc: Main procession through the streets of Ollantaytambo.

feria-huancaro.description: The largest agricultural, livestock, and craft fair in the Cusco region.
feria-huancaro.longDescription: The Huancaro Fair is the great showcase of Cusco's economic and cultural life. For a week, it brings together producers, artisans, and artists from all 13 provinces. It's a massive event with livestock exhibitions, sales of agricultural products, craft fairs, food courts, and live music concerts. It's an unmissable event to get to know the contemporary culture of Cusco.
feria-huancaro.history: The fair was established as the official event for the month of celebrations in Cusco. Its purpose is to promote regional economic activity and serve as a meeting point for urban and rural communities.

traditions.tradition_1: Judging of cattle and South American camelids.
traditions.tradition_2: Exhibition and sale of native potatoes and other Andean products.
traditions.tradition_3: Gastronomic area with typical dishes from all provinces.
traditions.tradition_4: Nightly concerts with national and international artists.

schedule.event_1_desc: The fairgrounds are open from morning until night with various activities.

wata-qallariy.description: Andean New Year and the beginning of the offerings to Pachamama (Mother Earth).
wata-qallariy.longDescription: Wata Qallariy marks the beginning of the Andean agricultural year. August 1st is the central day, when communities perform ceremonies of offering to Pachamama (Mother Earth) to thank her for her fruits and ask for a prosperous new agricultural cycle. It is a time of deep spiritual connection with the earth.
wata-qallariy.history: This is an ancient practice, predating the Incas, based on the Andean agricultural calendar. August is considered a sacred month when the earth 'opens up' to receive offerings.

traditions.tradition_1: Despacho' or offering ceremonies led by an 'altomisayoq' (Andean priest).
traditions.tradition_2: Burning of the offering to send the 'essence' to the Apus and Pachamama.
traditions.tradition_3: Communal meals and chicha drinking.

schedule.event_1_desc: Offering ceremonies are held in homes and on sacred mountains (Apus).

senor-de-huanca.location_detail: Sanctuary of Huanca, San Salvador, Calca
senor-de-huanca.description: A massive pilgrimage to the sanctuary of the Lord of Huanca.
senor-de-huanca.longDescription: The pilgrimage to the Lord of Huanca is one of the most important acts of faith in southern Peru. Thousands of devotees travel, many on foot, to the sanctuary located in a ravine near Cusco. They seek healing, miracles, and blessings from the image of a martyred Christ painted on a rock.
senor-de-huanca.history: According to tradition, in 1675, Jesus Christ appeared to a miner in a cave in Huanca. The local bishop ordered a painting of the scene on the rock, which became a place of worship. The devotion has grown exponentially since then.

traditions.tradition_1: Night pilgrimages from Cusco and other points.
traditions.tradition_2: Masses and blessing ceremonies for pilgrims and their vehicles.
traditions.tradition_3: Ritual baths in the stream that runs through the sanctuary.
traditions.tradition_4: Purchase of 'alasitas' (miniatures) representing the devotee's desires.

schedule.event_1_desc: The sanctuary receives pilgrims continuously, with masses and ceremonies throughout the day.

takanakuy-chumbivilcas.description: A ritual fighting festival to resolve conflicts and start the new year fresh.
takanakuy-chumbivilcas.longDescription: Takanakuy (Quechua for 'to hit each other') is a unique Christmas festival in the province of Chumbivilcas. Community members, dressed in elaborate costumes and masks, engage in public fistfights to settle personal disputes accumulated over the year. It's a socially sanctioned way to resolve conflicts and start the new year without grudges, followed by dancing and celebration.
takanakuy-chumbivilcas.history: Its origins are uncertain, but it is believed to be a tradition that mixes pre-Hispanic ritual combat with a colonial representation of justice. It is a cultural mechanism for conflict resolution in a region historically far from state control.

traditions.tradition_1: Dressing up as characters like the 'majeño', 'qarawatana', or 'negro'.
traditions.tradition_2: Public fights refereed by community authorities.
traditions.tradition_3: The 'wayliya', a festive music and dance that accompanies the celebration.
traditions.tradition_4: A hug and agreement to end the fight.

schedule.event_1_desc: The community gathers in the main square for the fights and subsequent celebrations.

fiesta-de-san-sebastian.description: A patronal feast with dances, processions, and a strong sense of local identity.
fiesta-de-san-sebastian.longDescription: The festival in honor of Saint Sebastian is the most important celebration in this traditional Cusco district. For several days, the streets are filled with folkloric dancers, music, and processions. The festival reinforces the local identity and the historical rivalry with the neighboring district of San Jerónimo.
fiesta-de-san-sebastian.history: The devotion to Saint Sebastian, protector against plagues, was established during the colonial era. The festival has incorporated many pre-Hispanic elements, especially in its dances and music.

traditions.tradition_1: Procession of the patron saint through the main streets.
traditions.tradition_2: Presentation of dance troupes, such as the 'Contradanza'.
traditions.tradition_3: Gastronomic fairs with typical local dishes.

schedule.event_1_desc: Main day with mass, procession, and dance presentations.

aniversario-de-quillabamba.description: The anniversary of the 'City of Eternal Summer', known for its coffee, cocoa, and festive atmosphere.
aniversario-de-quillabamba.longDescription: The anniversary of Quillabamba is the main festival of the province of La Convención. It is a week-long celebration that includes agricultural fairs, a Miss Coffee beauty pageant, motorcycle racing competitions, and large concerts with national artists. It reflects the vibrant and modern culture of Cusco's high jungle.
aniversario-de-quillabamba.history: The festival celebrates the founding of the city of Quillabamba. Over the years, it has become a showcase for the region's main products, especially coffee and cocoa.

traditions.tradition_1: The 'Miss Coffee' beauty pageant.
traditions.tradition_2: Tastings and sales of specialty coffees.
traditions.tradition_3: Motorcycle and motocross competitions.

schedule.event_1_desc: Multiple activities in different parts of the city.

uywa-chaka-y-chinu.description: A festival for the marking and fertility ritual of alpacas and llamas.
uywa-chaka-y-chinu.longDescription: Uywa Ch'aka y Ch'inu is an ancestral tradition in the high Andean communities of Espinar. It consists of marking the camelids (llamas and alpacas) with colorful tassels and performing rituals to ensure their fertility and health. It is a celebration of the deep bond between the Andean people and their animals.
uywa-chaka-y-chinu.history: This practice has pre-Hispanic origins and is fundamental to the livestock economy and worldview of the high Andean communities. It is a way of managing the herd and thanking the Apus for their protection.

traditions.tradition_1: The 'ch'inu' or tying of colorful tassels on the animals' ears.
traditions.tradition_2: Ritual offerings with coca leaves and chicha.
traditions.tradition_3: Music and dance to celebrate the herd's fertility.
traditions.tradition_4: The 't'inka', a ritual toast with chicha.

schedule.event_1_desc: The ritual is performed within each family or community.

navidad-cusquena-santurantikuy.location_detail: The main fair is in the Plaza de Armas, but Christmas is celebrated throughout the city.
navidad-cusquena-santurantikuy.description: The most important Christmas fair in Peru, where artisans sell traditional nativity figures.
navidad-cusquena-santurantikuy.longDescription: Santurantikuy, which means 'Sale of Saints' in Quechua, is a magical Christmas fair that takes over Cusco's Plaza de Armas every December 24th. Hundreds of artisans from all over the region come to sell handcrafted images for nativity scenes, with the 'Niño Manuelito' (the baby Jesus) being the central figure. It's a vibrant expression of art, faith, and tradition that is essential to the Cusco Christmas.
navidad-cusquena-santurantikuy.history: Its origins date back to the colonial era, when the Spanish introduced the tradition of nativity scenes. The Andean artisans adopted this custom, creating unique figures that blend Catholic iconography with local elements and worldview. Over the centuries, Santurantikuy has become the largest folk art fair in Peru.

traditions.tradition_1: The sale and exhibition of handcrafted 'Niño Manuelitos' in countless styles.
traditions.tradition_2: Creation of complete nativity scenes with moss, plants, and miniature animals.
traditions.tradition_3: Drinking 'ponche', a hot, sweet drink to combat the cold.
traditions.tradition_4: The fair lasts until late at night on Christmas Eve.

schedule.event_1_desc: Santurantikuy Fair in the Plaza de Armas. Artisans set up from the early morning hours.

Virgen-Natividad-Paruro.description: A deeply rooted religious festival celebrating the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, known for its traditional dances and devotion.
Virgen-Natividad-Paruro.longDescription: The Feast of the Virgen de la Natividad in Paruro is one of the most significant religious and cultural expressions in the Cusco region. It takes place every September 7th, 8th, and 9th, with the 8th being the central day. The celebration combines Catholic fervor with Andean ancestral traditions, featuring masses, processions, and impressive folk dance performances that fill the streets with color and music.
Virgen-Natividad-Paruro.history: The devotion to the Nativity of Mary in Paruro dates back to the colonial era. The image of the Virgin is considered highly miraculous, attracting thousands of faithful. The festivities have evolved over the centuries, incorporating traditional dances like the 'Siqllas' and 'Qapaq Negro', becoming a symbol of the local cultural identity.

traditions.tradition_1: The main procession of the image of the Virgen de la Natividad through the streets of Paruro.
traditions.tradition_2: The execution of various traditional dances ('Danzas Autóctonas'), each with its own costume and meaning.
traditions.tradition_3: The 'Víspera' (Eve) on September 7th, marked by firecrackers and music, signaling the start of the central celebration.
traditions.tradition_4: Masses and religious ceremonies held in the Temple of the Nativity.

schedule.event_1_desc: Víspera (Eve) of the Feast with traditional music, fireworks, and the 'entrada' (entry) of the dance groups.
schedule.event_2_desc: Central Day of the Feast. Solemn Mass and the main procession of the Virgen de la Natividad.
schedule.event_3_desc: The 'Och' (farewell) of the Virgin and final ceremonies, including the culmination of the dance presentations.

festividad-santaCecilia.location_detail: Temple and Parish of Nuestra Señora de la Almudena, Santiago district, Cusco.
festividad-santaCecilia.description: A celebration in honor of the patron saint of musicians, marked by special masses and musical tributes.
festividad-santaCecilia.longDescription: The Feast of Santa Cecilia, virgin and martyr, is commemorated in Cusco on November 22, although the liturgical acts and tributes usually begin on the eve (November 21). This is a day when the city's musicians—from orchestras, bands, choirs, and folkloric associations—gather to pay tribute to their patron saint. In the Temple of Almudena, which houses a very active parish community, this celebration includes a special mass for musicians, where their instruments are blessed, and thanks are given for the art of music that accompanies the faith.
festividad-santaCecilia.history: Saint Cecilia of Rome is a martyr from the early centuries of Christianity. Tradition holds that while musicians played at her wedding, she sang to God in her heart, which is why she is attributed the patronage of music. Her cult spread from Europe. In Cusco, the celebration integrated into the religious festivities, becoming a meeting point for musical guilds and academies seeking her protection and inspiration for their art.

traditions.tradition_1: Thanksgiving or Tribute Mass, dedicated to the musicians and their families.
traditions.tradition_2: Blessing of musical instruments (organs, quenas, charangos, violins, etc.) during the Mass.
traditions.tradition_3: Musical performances and serenades by bands and orchestras in front of the temple or in the atrium.
traditions.tradition_4: Confraternity gatherings and special lunches organized by the musicians' guilds.

schedule.event_1_desc: Vigil (Víspera) of Saint Cecilia. There may be serenades and initial musical demonstrations in honor of the Saint.
schedule.event_2_desc: Central and solemn Mass in honor of Saint Cecilia, with the active participation of musicians and choirs.
schedule.event_3_desc: Tribute acts, musical presentations, and procession of the Saint's image (if there is one in that temple).

chumbivilcas-horses.location_detail: Chuñuhuiri Sector of the Hanansaya Orccoma Peasant Community, Santo Tomás district.
chumbivilcas-horses.description: Chumbivilcas National Horse Racing Contest, a central event held for the province's anniversary.
chumbivilcas-horses.longDescription: The contest is a fundamental activity to re-evaluate the equestrian hobby, protect the cultural richness, and the customary identity of the 'Land of the Qorilazos.' It attracts the participation of local breeders and studs, as well as those from various provinces in Cusco and neighboring southern Peruvian regions such as Puno, Arequipa, Apurímac, and Ayacucho. Horses compete in various categories, covering distances between 400 meters and 1000 meters.
chumbivilcas-horses.history: The equestrian tradition in Santo Tomás, as in all of Chumbivilcas, is intrinsically linked to the 'Qorilazo' (the Andean cowboy), being a manifestation of courage and skill on horseback. The 1st National Horse Racing Contest was held in 2023 for the 198th Anniversary of the Province's Political Creation. Additionally, interregional horse racing contests are held during Easter (April), and events have been announced for the Bicentennial (2025).

traditions.tradition_1: Horse races in the High Andean (horses without genetic improvement), Improved, and Open categories.
traditions.tradition_2: Competition between studs (horses) coming from various provinces and regions of the southern part of the country.
traditions.tradition_3: Revitalization of the local economy with the sale of gastronomy and local products by community members.
traditions.tradition_4: Award ceremony for the winning owners by the Municipal Council.

schedule.event_1_desc: Start of the equestrian competition with qualifying races and the participation of the studs.
schedule.event_2_desc: Continuation and culmination of the equestrian contest with the finals and the award ceremony in various categories.
